essentialQuestion.source: How can you tell if a photo, video or voice is real?
essentialQuestion.back: How can you know whether a photo, video or voice is real?

learningGoal.source: Explain how AI can make realistic pictures, videos and voices, and check the source before you trust or share one.
learningGoal.back: Explain how AI can produce realistic pictures, videos and voices, and check the source before you believe or share it.

read.sections.0.heading.source: AI can make pictures, videos and voices
read.sections.0.heading.back: AI can produce pictures, videos and voices

read.sections.0.text.source: Some AI tools can create new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from enormous numbers of real examples, so what they make can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly for art, films or education, and explain that AI made the work. A fake is different: it pretends to show something real that never happened. A deepfake is a fake that copies a real person's face or voice, often to trick people for money or attention. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a talking goat with the label “Made with AI, just for fun”. Someone else posted a photo of a pumpkin as big as a car. Is it real?
read.sections.0.text.back: Some AI tools can create new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from huge numbers of real examples, so what they produce can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly for art, films or education, and explain that AI produced the work. Fake content, on the other hand, is different: it pretends to show something real that never happened. A deepfake is fake content that copies the face or voice of a real person, often to trick people for money or attention. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a talking goat with the label “Made with AI, just for fun”. Someone else posted a photo of a pumpkin as big as a car. Is that photo real?
read.sections.0.text.note: "A fake" (noun) is "kandungan palsu" (fake content), so the glossary word "palsu" is marked. "Deepfake" is kept in English, as Malaysian news uses it (shared TERMS.md).

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Some AI tools make new pictures, videos and voices. They learned from lots of real examples. So the new ones look realistic. Some people say openly that AI made their art or lessons. A fake is different. It shows something that never happened, as if it were real. A deepfake copies a real person's face or voice to trick people. In Greenhill, the comedy club's talking goat says AI made it. But is the huge pumpkin real?
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Some AI tools produce new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from many real examples. So what they produce looks realistic. Some people say openly that AI produced their art or lessons. Fake content is different. It shows something that never happened, as if it were real. A deepfake copies the face or voice of a real person to trick people. In Greenhill, the comedy club's talking goat states that AI produced it. But is the big pumpkin real?

read.sections.1.heading.source: Strange details are clues, not proof
read.sections.1.heading.back: Strange details are clues, not proof

read.sections.1.text.source: AI pictures sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, messy letters on a sign or a background that melts into a wall. In a video, the mouth may not move with the words. These details can be clues, but they are not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so a fake can look perfect. Real photographs can also look strange, for example when they are blurry or taken in poor light. In a 2025 study, participants wrongly labelled about one in four real photographs as AI-made. The fruit seller's photo has very smooth skin, but the photo club says a phone took it.
read.sections.1.text.back: AI pictures sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, jumbled letters on a sign or a background that seems to melt into a wall. In a video, the mouth may not move with the words. These details can be clues, but not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so fake content can look perfect. Real photos can also look strange, for example when the photo is blurry or taken in dim light. In a study in 2025, participants wrongly labelled about one in four real photos as made by AI. The fruit seller's photo shows very smooth skin, but the photography club says a phone took it.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Petunjuk" (clue) is also the Malay word for "hint" in Lesson 11 and for "map key" in Our World; context makes it clear here.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: AI pictures sometimes have mistakes, like six fingers or messy letters. These are clues. But clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. Real photos can look strange too, when they are dark or not sharp. In a 2025 study, people looked at real photos. They called about one in four of them AI-made. The fruit seller has very smooth skin. But a phone took that photo.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: AI pictures sometimes have mistakes, such as six fingers or jumbled letters. These are clues. But clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. Real photos can also look strange, when they are dark or not clear. In a study in 2025, people looked at real photos. They thought about one in four of those photos were made by AI. The fruit seller has very smooth skin. But a phone took that photo.

read.sections.2.text.source: The most useful check is the source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from? Do other trusted sources show the same thing? The farm's own page says it grew no giant pumpkin, so that photo is probably fake. The rain photo came from the market's own page, and other people posted the same rain, so it is probably real. For a voice message, contact the person in another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her in person. If you still can't tell, say so, and don't share it yet.
read.sections.2.text.back: The most useful check is its source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from? Do other trusted sources show the same thing? The farm's own page says the farm did not grow a giant pumpkin, so that photo is probably fake. The rain photo came from the market's own page, and other people posted the same rain, so that photo is probably real. For a voice message, contact the person in another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her face to face. If you are still not sure, say so, and do not share it yet.

watch.summary.source: This video comes from a series made with a team of teenage fact-checkers. It explains that some people use AI to make fake pictures, videos and sounds. They often do it to get money, attention or power. The video shows clues to look for. AI pictures can have strange hands, odd shadows and strange backgrounds. In AI videos, look for edges that blur or flicker. Check the shadows, and check if the lips move with the words. For AI voices, listen to the tone and to the sounds in the background. The video also shows tools that can help, like a search that finds where else a picture appears online. But these tools are not always right. A person still needs to think and check before sharing.
watch.summary.back: This video is from a series made together with a team of teenage fact-checkers. This video explains that some people use AI to produce fake pictures, videos and sounds. They often do it to get money, attention or power. This video shows clues to look for. AI pictures may have strange hands, odd shadows and strange backgrounds. In AI videos, look for edges that blur or flicker. Check the shadows, and check whether the lips move with the words. For AI voices, listen to the tone and the sounds in the background. This video also shows tools that can help, such as a search that finds other places the picture appears online. But these tools are not always right. A human still needs to think and check before sharing it.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Deepfakes are used to hurt real people: fake pictures that shame someone, fake videos of leaders, and cloned voices in scams (for example a call that sounds like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). The lesson keeps its examples silly on purpose. Don't show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says a fake was made of them or someone they know, don't discuss the details in class; follow the partner's own safeguarding process.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Deepfakes are used to hurt real people: fake pictures that shame someone, fake videos of leaders, and cloned voices in scams (for example a call that sounds like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). This lesson keeps its examples funny on purpose. Do not show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says fake content has been made about them or someone they know, do not discuss the details in class; follow the partner organisation's own child safeguarding process.

educatorNotes.0.source: Teach checking first: who posted it, when, where it first came from, whether other trusted sources show the same thing, and for a voice, contacting the person another way. Visual glitches (extra fingers, messy letters, smooth skin) are reasons to check, never proof: newer tools make fewer of them, and real photos can show odd details too. In a 2025 study (Kamali and others, CHI '25), people correctly called real photographs real 74% of the time, so about one in four were wrongly called AI-made. Accept “can't tell yet” as a strong answer; the activity has no score. Paper version: the six posts on cards, sorted under the four headings.
educatorNotes.0.back: Teach checking first: who posted it, when, where it first came from, whether other trusted sources show the same thing, and for a voice, contacting the person another way. Visual flaws (extra fingers, jumbled letters, smooth skin) are reasons to check, never proof: newer tools produce fewer flaws, and real photos can also show odd details. In a study in 2025 (Kamali and colleagues, CHI '25), people correctly said real photos were real 74% of the time, so about one in four were wrongly thought to be made by AI. Accept “cannot be sure yet” as a strong answer; this activity has no marks. Paper version: six posts on cards, sorted under four headings.

educatorNotes.1.source: Labelled AI work (art, films, lessons, a joke clearly marked “Made with AI”) is not the same as a fake that pretends to be real or copies a real person. Labels can be lost when a picture is reposted (News Literacy Project, 2026), so a labelled post can become misleading when shared without it. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check viral pictures and videos, and Mafindo says AI-based hoaxes are getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). A teacher with internet can show one checked example; learners don't need to go online.
educatorNotes.1.back: Labelled AI work (art, films, lessons, a joke clearly marked “Made with AI”) is not the same as fake content that pretends to be real or copies a real person. Labels can be lost when a picture is posted again (News Literacy Project, 2026), so a labelled post can become misleading when shared without that label. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check viral pictures and videos, and Mafindo states that AI-based fake news is getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). A teacher who has internet can show one example that has been checked; learners do not need to go online.
